tools.title: ☢️ Trump is radioactively unpopular
tools.summary_raw: Embracing Jensen Huang might hurt Huang more than it helps the president. Plus, listener questions on Still Counting EP14.
tools.content_text: Donald Trump after returning to the White House from Walter Reed National Military Medical Center on Oct. 5, 2020. Win McNamee/Getty Images. Happy Thanksgiving Eve! I think we have a good little newsletter for you today, but let me link to this week’s Still Counting episode first: Video above, audio below. In case you’re stuck on the tarmac somewhere , we tried to have some fun, talking about the Trump-backed restoration of Jensen Huang at Nvidia , the Democrats’ debate schedule , and answering several listener questions. And yes, our Thanksgiving wish is that you’ll comment, like , review and/or subscribe to the show. The context President Trump’s approval rating has steadily declined over the past two years. Believe me: we get some things wrong around these parts. We have before and we will again. But the idea that second terms hit different and have much lower approval floors was one of those points on which we were a little ahead of the curve. Subscribe now On the podcast, we talked about how poorly Trump has performed as some kind of “populist”. I’m sorry if any of this comes across as partisan, but I’m trying to describe reality. In various ways, he’s betrayed his base. The “Liberation Day” tariffs triggered an initial decline in Trump’s numbers, but at least they were broadly consistent with what he’d promised on the campaign trail. Going to war with Iran and spiking gas prices as a result wasn’t what he advertised, however. I don’t want to overindex on this , but talking a big game about releasing the Epstein files and then basically reneging wasn’t consistent with his promises either. And then there’s this Nvidia story — and the broader embrace of Silicon Valley by the president and vice versa . Look, I respect Jensen Huang, and I don’t care who he slept with. Silicon Valley types almost seem to be promoting angles about his reported infidelity or his reported abusive treatment of staffers because it obscures the real issue here: that Nvidia’s best chips were reportedly winding up in the hands of China . AI is the most important technology of my lifetime , and one of the most important in the history of the human species. It also plausibly follows winner-take-all dynamics, and it obviously has national security implications . I don’t think Huang’s position is incoherent. Maybe American leadership in the sector is so strong that we can afford to export Blackwell chips to China because we’re not going to forsake the lead. And maybe AI is a “normal technology ,” as I think Huang and Nvidia honestly believe — although I don’t think they have much remaining credibility on the matter. But Trump ran as a “China hawk. ” Because I basically do think that AI is an extraordinary technology , and I’d put nuclear weapons in the same category, I’m going to make the obvious comparison here. tools.title: AI is moving way too fast
tools.summary_raw: I think AI coding tools are miraculous. So why do I feel so unsettled?
tools.content_text: (Getty Images/Silver Bulletin illustration) I’m not even sure where to start. So I’ll begin by quoting Scott Aaronson , the computer scientist, from his post after OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem in September: My position on AI is merely the conservative, skeptical position of 2006, updated with intellectual honesty for the reality of late 2026. And that position, if you need me to spell it out, is as follows: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA The thing is, I would have sworn the Navier-Stokes proof and Aaronson’s post happened longer ago than they did: Wasn’t that in June or July, maybe back when the World Cup was going on? Nope, it was barely two months ago. I more precisely remember the date 1 of another AI inflection point: in February, when the White House designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk . That was a different kind of story, about the intersections between AI, politics and national security, rather than the progress of the technology per se . But that also feels much longer ago. A lot has happened since then. The United States went to war with Iran. Democrats won in the biggest midterm landslide in 50 years . (Also, in truly important news, the Knicks won the NBA championship. ) The implications of the midterms are vast, and the newly elected members won’t be seated until January — but hell, even Nov. 3 is starting to feel like a long time ago. Because over the past three weeks, the news has been fucking crazy. Share On Nov. 12, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after he acknowledged an affair with a woman reported to be a Chinese spy. Last week, Anthropic had the largest IPO in history . Then the next day, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpoge announced that, using a superpowered version of Claude, he’d identified a solution to an even more challenging mathematical problem: the Riemann hypothesis. 2 Then, on Monday morning, under pressure from President Trump, Nvidia announced it had restored Huang as CEO, sending its stock up more than 30 percent and putting the broader NASDAQ so far ahead that trading on NASDAQ-100 futures briefly had to be halted because they triggered a “circuit breaker”. I’ve been in the news business for a long time. There’s not supposed to be this much news this quickly. And nobody seems to know what to make of it: Anthropic’s share price has already fallen by around 25 percent since its debut in public markets last week. I can vouch for how fast AI is progressing, at least when it comes to coding As much as I don’t want to commingle what’s important to the broader world with what’s important to our business at Silver Bulletin, it’s hard not to, because there’s a common thread: AI. market.title: IRE Voices: Betty Medsger on publishing stolen FBI files
market.summary_raw: IRE Voices: Betty Medsger on publishing stolen FBI files "I never felt afraid…I was very concerned about the people who burglarized the FBI office and sent me the files they had stolen [because their fingerprints might have been on the pages and envelope]…so I destroyed the original copies to make sure that I was in…
market.content_text: IRE Voices: Betty Medsger on publishing stolen FBI files "I never felt afraid…I was very concerned about the people who burglarized the FBI office and sent me the files they had stolen [because their fingerprints might have been on the pages and envelope]…so I destroyed the original copies to make sure that I was in a position to protect my sources if I ever—if what I had ever ended up in the wrong hands," says Betty Medsger in an interview with IRE. In March 1971, Medsger, then a Washington Post reporter, received what would come to be known as the Media files. Stolen from the FBI office in Media, PA, the packet of files included a cover letter explaining that the files came from the Citizens Commission to Investigate the FBI. The Commission, risking decades in prison, burglarized the Media office to discover evidence of the FBI's suppression of dissent, which they considered a crime against democracy. At the time, there was no official oversight for the FBI or similar agencies. The eight members of the self-appointed commission never were caught and remained anonymous until the 2014 publication of Medsger's book, The Burglary: The Discovery of J. Edgar Hoover’s Secret FBI. The files revealed massive illegal surveillance operations conducted particularly against Black Americans, who were targeted not due to criminal suspicion but racial discrimination. The FBI’s worst operations, COINTELPRO, were revealed in these files. These secret operations were designed to “disrupt and neutralize” people Hoover regarded as subversive. They ranged from crude to cruel and even included murder. Of the five people who received the files—two members of Congress, a reporter at The New York Times, a reporter at The Los Angeles Times, and Medsger—only Medsger published the content of the files. The other recipients returned the files to the FBI. The decision to publish was difficult for Washington Post publisher Katharine Graham; it was the first time the Nixon administration demanded she suppress a story. These revelations by Medsger and the Post led to the first congressional investigations of the FBI and all intelligence agencies, and were part of a shift from journalists protecting the secrets of such agencies to holding them accountable. When Medsger received the files, she did not consider herself an investigative reporter. “I was just a reporter dealing with what came my way,” she says. That changed by the time IRE was formed. Medsger became a founding member and "...realized that [investigative reporting] was wonderful work." She says, "IRE expanded what I saw as possible for me and others, including my future students, to do." Medsger became a journalist overnight in 1964. Planning to teach high school in the fall, shortly after graduating from college in January, she applied for a job as a filing clerk at the local newspaper. […]

market.title: Blocking, charging and licensing: How Kleine Zeitung and KG Media manage bot access
market.summary_raw: Indonesia's KG Media and Austria’s Kleine Zeitung could not be more different. They vary in scale, market size, audience profile and organisational structure. But they share a common challenge: bot traffic.
market.content_text: The recent Asian Media Leaders Summit brought diverse publishers together to talk strategy and how they were responding to market disruption. Xenia Daum , CEO of Austria’s Kleine Zeitung, and Andy Budiman of Indonesia’s KG Media shared how their organisations were responding to AI companies’ accelerating demand for publisher content. Kleine Zeitung is Austria’s largest regional news publisher, owned by the Styria Media Group. Its print and online editions serve communities in the Austrian states of Styria and Carinthia – which have a combined population of 1.8-million people. It reaches a third of the population via print, and almost 43% though either its print or digital products. KG Media is a sprawling Indonesian media conglomerate with interests in TV, online, print and radio. In its heyday the group’s flagship newspaper, Kompas, reached 1% of Indonesia’s population. “But today, even addressing 1% of the 286-million population on digital directly, is a heavy task,” said Budiman. “..our goal is to address the top of the population, which actually controls the majority of the economy in Indonesia.” Kleine Zeitung’s accelerating bot traffic Kleine Zeitung recorded nearly 70 million bot requests over three months, with regional articles among the most frequently crawled content. AI bot traffic is accelerating month by month according to figures from its recently introduced TollBit paywall – moving from 2.7% of total traffic to 4.4% in three months to October. Daum regards AI-companies as Frenemies: “We can’t avoid them, we have to work with them.” But the challenge for a small publisher like Kleine Zeitung was getting access to the AI companies – something TollBit offers. The paywall now blocks all bots by default, but then identifies them and interrogates what they want to do with the content, distinguishing between access covered by existing permissions, such as subscriber access or authorised arrangements, and commercial third-party use. Kleine Zeitung has also introduced a machine-readable, structured versions of its website content. It is charging for access not covered by an existing subscription or agreement, with potential CPM-based pricing influenced by factors such as the freshness and uniqueness of the content. “We try to find the right CPM for the right bot, at the right moment,” Daum says. Older archive material may have less value to AI companies than recent reporting. Not all bots are treated alike Kleine Zeitung distinguishes between crawlers that may bring referral traffic and those that extract content without generating meaningful visits to the publisher’s website. Daum said Kleine Zeitung had blocked Amazon’s bot because, in her account, it extracted content without bringing human traffic and had not agreed to pay for access. […]

market.title: The Wall Street Journal joins a growing list of publishers disallowing bots by default
market.summary_raw: One of the world’s largest business publishers is shutting the door on unwelcome bots. In May, Dow Jones overhauled its bot strategy and now disallows all bots by default, the company told Nieman Lab. The new bot permissions apply to all of its free and paid consumer news sites, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s,...
market.content_text: One of the world’s largest business publishers is shutting the door on unwelcome bots. In May, Dow Jones overhauled its bot strategy and now disallows all bots by default, the company told Nieman Lab. The new bot permissions apply to all of its free and paid consumer news sites, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, and MarketWatch. As part of the shift, the company revised each site’s robots.txt file — a webpage that tells bots which parts of a site they can and can’t access. Rather than reactively blacklisting bots through robots.txt, Dow Jones now operates with a whitelist for select crawlers and scrapers. “As bot traffic has shifted from discovery-oriented use cases toward systems that can ingest, summarize, or otherwise benefit from our content without a relationship in place, we have moved to a more deliberate signal,” said Nolly Evans , chief development officer at Dow Jones. “[This] signals to third parties that they must negotiate and partner directly with us for content access.” The Wall Street Journal’s whitelist contains more than 60 bots, including search engine crawlers and three scrapers operated by OpenAI, which has a $250 million-plus licensing deal with Dow Jones’ parent company, News Corp. “We’re seeing astronomical growth in bot traffic while human referrals and traffic to news sites are being curtailed,” said Evans. “That’s a clear signal to publishers that the old norms are no longer working, and that something needs to change.” Robots.txt files are voluntary guidance for all bots, including those deployed by AI companies. They’re not hard technical blocks or legally binding contracts. Some AI companies, like Perplexity, have used “stealth crawlers” to bypass robots.txt files while evading detection. Still, The Journal isn’t alone in using robots.txt to disallow bots by default, whether to create friction for scrapers, as leverage to negotiate for content licensing deals, or to minimize the burden on their servers. An analysis of the robots.txt files of 1,000 leading English-language publishers websites by the bot analytics company Known Agents shows that about 2% of those sites now disallow all bots by default, including Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Publishers Weekly, and the British technology news site The Register. Many of these publications are owned by News Corp, including several of the company’s Australian newspapers (The Australian, The Daily Telegraph in Sydney, the Herald Sun in Melbourne) and its marquee U.K. papers (The Times, The Sun, The Scottish Sun). “One of the most important issues for us is making sure that the IP journalists create is respected by the AI companies,” News Corp CEO Robert Thomson said in an interview with CNBC last week. “The principled companies want to have an agreement, and the unprincipled companies don’t. market.title: Confident kids, cautious elders: What we get wrong (and right) about who really understands social media algorithms
market.summary_raw: Ask a 19-year-old how TikTok decides what to show them, and you’ll likely get a fast, confident answer about watch time, likes, and how “the algorithm just gets me.” Ask their grandmother, and you’re more likely to get a shrug. The scene fits a story we’ve been telling for years: Young people are “digital natives”...
market.content_text: Ask a 19-year-old how TikTok decides what to show them, and you’ll likely get a fast, confident answer about watch time, likes, and how “the algorithm just gets me.” Ask their grandmother, and you’re more likely to get a shrug. The scene fits a story we’ve been telling for years: Young people are “digital natives” who intuitively grasp the platforms they grew up on, while older adults are outsiders, left behind and vulnerable. That story matters more than it used to. Algorithmically curated platforms are now a major source of news for Americans of all ages , which means people’s sense of how those systems work shapes how they judge the information they get there. But when you test what each group actually knows, rather than what they say they know, the story doesn’t hold up. In a piece last year for Nieman Lab, I reported that young adults who spent more time on social media tended to know less about how algorithms work, and I speculated that constant use might create an illusion of understanding. My recent study published in New Media & Society set out to test that idea directly — measuring not just what people know, but how confident they are about it — across the full adult age range. Surveying 1,205 U.S. adults ages 18 to 65 and older, I measured two things. First, I asked people to rate their own understanding of how algorithms select, rank, and personalize content. Second, I measured their actual awareness of how these systems work, which covers content filtering, automated decision-making, data use, and algorithmic bias. The self-ratings matched the conventional wisdom: Younger respondents rated their understanding significantly higher than older respondents did. But the awareness scores did not. Across every age group, actual awareness of how algorithms function was essentially flat. In other words, the generational edge that shows up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge. To capture this, I use the concept “algorithmic knowledge confidence”: the gap between what people believe they know and what they can demonstrate. When self-assessment outpaces actual awareness, that’s overconfidence; when it lags behind, that’s underconfidence. Young adults tended toward the former: They don’t necessarily understand algorithms better, but they feel more certain that they do. Older adults tended toward the latter: They don’t know less, but they’re more cautious about claiming what they know. Then why would the most-online generation feel the surest? Psychologists have long documented that people mistake familiarity for understanding. When something feels easy to process — often simply because we’ve encountered it many times — we tend to assume we understand it. This is called processing fluency. Exposure to social media differs sharply by age. […]
